narrative:
The model estimates a 10% chance that you will fail the final year. That is a low but non-zero risk estimate, not a certainty, so the remedial courses should be treated as a safeguard: the school is requiring support because the model still sees some risk that you may not pass.

The strongest factor in the prediction was your past record of class failures. You have none, which matches the average for students who passed, and this pushed the prediction toward passing. The next most important factor was your intention to continue to higher education. Wanting higher education is shared by all students in the passing comparison group, so this also worked in your favor. Third was your weekly study time. You study 2–5 hours, the most common pattern among passing students, at about 55%, and this too pushed toward passing rather than failing. Each of the top three signals was protective, so the 10% fail estimate reflects a smaller remaining risk rather than a strong forecast of failure.

To improve further, consider increasing study time above 5 hours where possible, keeping attendance at zero absences, and using the remedial courses to check weaker subjects. Continue aiming for higher education and maintain your no-failure record.
